info.name: Task Queue
info.description:
Ready-to-run collection for the PostgreSQL task queue.

## Before you start
1. Start the stack: `npm start` (API and dashboard on :3000, one worker on the `jobs` queue).
2. If your API is elsewhere, change the `baseUrl` collection variable.
3. Run the folders top-to-bottom (Collection Runner works) — later requests reuse ids captured by earlier ones.

## How it's organised
- **1. Health & discovery** — liveness and the queue list.
- **2. Enqueue & run (worker executes)** — uses the `jobs` queue; the running worker actually runs each handler, so `GET /tasks/:id` shows a real result. Re-send the "get result" request after ~1s if the task hasn't been picked up yet.
- **3. Claim → heartbeat → ack** and **4. Retry → DLQ → requeue** — use the `demo` queue, which **no worker consumes**, so these requests drive the whole lifecycle (claim, lease, nack, backoff, dead-letter, replay) by hand with no race against the worker.
- **5. Idempotent enqueue** — two enqueues with one `dedupeKey` collapse to one task.
- **6. Validation & errors** — the negative cases: problem+json shapes and every status code the API uses.
- **7. Load generator** — bulk-enqueues into `demo` so the dashboard's `ready` count visibly climbs.

`X-Worker-Id` is required only on the worker surface — `claim`, `ack`, `nack`, `extend` — where it names the worker whose lease is being asserted. Producers (enqueue), reads and requeue send none. It identifies a caller; it does not authenticate one. The service assumes a private network.

request.description: Liveness: `{ status: 'ok', lastReaperTickAt }`. The timestamp is the lease reaper's heartbeat (it ticks every ~15s, half the 30s lease), so a stalled recovery loop is visible. No worker header.
`{ queues: string[] }` — every queue that exists, sorted by name: those seeded from `queues.json` plus any created implicitly by a first enqueue. Backs the UI's queue list.

item.name: 2. Enqueue & run (worker executes) — queue: jobs
item.description: Requires the worker started by `npm start`. It runs each handler for real, so the result is retrievable after ack. Enqueue needs no `X-Worker-Id`.

request.description:
Body: `{ type, payload, delay?, dedupeKey? }` — `delay` in ms (0–7 days), `dedupeKey` 1–256 chars. Unknown fields are rejected (422).

`js` payload: `{ source, input?, timeoutMs? }`. `source` is the body of an `async function (input)`, run in a forked child (scrubbed environment, 128 MB heap cap, hard timeout — `timeoutMs` 1–300000, default 30s); its return value, JSON round-tripped, becomes the result. Expect `result: 5` once the worker has it.

201 with `{ id }` when a task was created; 200 with the surviving task's `{ id }` when a `dedupeKey` collapsed it onto an existing one.

exec: console.log('state is ' + t.state + ' — re-send in ~1s for the result');

request.description:
`{ id, queue, type, payload, state, attempts, maxAttempts, result, failureKind, lastError, createdAt, succeededAt, failedAt }`. `state` is one of `ready | in_flight | succeeded | dlq`, derived from the row *and* the lease clock: an in-flight task whose lease has lapsed already reads as `ready` (or `dlq` if attempts are exhausted) before the reaper touches it.

If `state` is still `ready`/`in_flight`, re-send after ~1 second — the worker polls on a short cadence. The claim fence (`claimId`) is never returned here: reading a task must not confer the ability to ack it.

`llm` payload: `{ model, prompt }` — both non-empty strings; `model` is not checked against a catalogue. The provider is a deterministic stub behind an interface — no API key or network — so the result is `{ model, content: 'stub(<model>): <first 64 chars of prompt>' }`; the call path, classification and result capture are real. Prefixing the prompt with `FAIL:rate_limit`, `FAIL:server` or `FAIL:timeout` injects a retryable failure; `FAIL:auth` or `FAIL:refusal` a terminal one.

`http` payload: `{ method, url, headers?, body?, timeoutMs? }` — method one of GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE/HEAD, `http`/`https` URL only. The handler captures status and body (cut at 256 KiB and flagged `truncated`). The SSRF guard resolves the host, rejects private/loopback/link-local/metadata ranges against the resolved IP, pins that IP for the connection and re-checks on every redirect — so a public URL is required, and the worker needs outbound internet. `429`, `5xx`, resets and timeouts retry; other `4xx` and blocked targets dead-letter. The worker sends `Idempotency-Key: <task id>` on the outbound request unless the payload's `headers` already carry one, so a receiver that honours the header sees a redelivered attempt as the same request.

`{ ready, inFlight, dlq }`. `ready` includes delayed and backing-off tasks and expired leases not yet reaped; `inFlight` counts only live leases. Counted from partial indexes, and held equal to the `task_state` view by a named invariant test. 404 for a queue that does not exist.

item.name: 3. Claim → heartbeat → ack — queue: demo
item.description: No worker consumes `demo`, so these requests are the consumer: claim a task, renew its lease, then ack it. Claims use `max: 1` so nothing is left in flight with a lease nobody renews.

request.description: The `demo` queue is created implicitly on first enqueue, with the default policy: 5 attempts, backoff base 3s, cap 5min, dedupe window 10min. A queue named in `queues.json` keeps its own policy instead.

Body `{ workerId, max }` (`max` 1–100), plus `X-Worker-Id`; body and header must agree (422 otherwise). Atomically claims up to `max` ready tasks, oldest `run_after` first, in one `UPDATE ... FROM (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)` — concurrent claimers step over each other's rows instead of blocking, and no task is handed to two workers. Each claim counts an attempt and grants a 30s lease.

Response: `{ tasks: [{ id, type, payload, attempts, claimId, leaseUntil }], leaseUntil }`. `claimId` is a fresh UUID per claim — the fence that ack/nack/extend may echo so a stale execution cannot act on a task since re-claimed. Empty queue (or unknown queue) → 200 with `tasks: []` and `leaseUntil: null`, never 404.

Body `{ workerId, claimId? }`; `workerId` must equal `X-Worker-Id` (422 otherwise). Renews the lease by another 30s from now and returns `{ leaseUntil }`. 409 `lost-lease` if the task is not in flight under this worker and claim, or once the task has been in flight longer than the 5-minute execution budget — the server holds that bound, so a handler that heartbeats forever cannot hold a task forever.

Body `{ result?, claimId? }` — both optional, an empty body is fine. Marks the task `succeeded` and stores `result` (any JSON up to 256 KiB; larger is refused with 413 and is terminal for the task). 204 on success. Retrying the same ack after success returns 409 `lost-lease`: ack is deliberately not idempotent, since the caller has released the task either way and at-least-once already covers the ambiguity.

exec: pm.test('result was stored', () => pm.expect(t.result).to.eql({ ok: true, note: 'acked via Postman' }));

request.description: The stored result survives after ack; `succeededAt` is set.

item.name: 4. Retry → DLQ → requeue — queue: demo
item.description: A retryable nack (the default) sends the task back to `ready` with exponential, fully jittered backoff; a terminal nack dead-letters it immediately, whatever attempts remain; requeue replays it from the DLQ and resets the attempt count. Two tasks: one to retry, one to dead-letter, because the retried one is not claimable again until its backoff elapses.

request.description:
Body `{ reason, retryable?, forgiveAttempt?, kind?, claimId? }`. `retryable` omitted defaults to **true**, so the brief's bare `{ reason }` gets the brief's behaviour: back to `ready` after a backoff of `random(0, min(cap, base × 4^attempts))` — with the default policy [0, 12s) after the first attempt, then [0, 48s), [0, 192s), [0, 5min) — until attempts are exhausted, when the task dead-letters. The attempt stays counted.

`kind` (the closed `failureKind` set) is derived when omitted: `handler_error` here, `handler_terminal` for `retryable: false`, `worker_shutdown` for `forgiveAttempt: true`. `forgiveAttempt` is the blameless release a draining worker sends: back to `ready` at once, the attempt uncounted. When `kind` is sent it must agree with `retryable` (`handler_terminal`, `timeout`, `unclassified`, `result_too_large`, `no_handler`, `lease_expired` are terminal; `handler_error` and `worker_shutdown` retry), otherwise 422.

exec: pm.test('classified as a retryable handler error', () => pm.expect(t.failureKind).to.eql('handler_error'));

request.description: `ready` again, with `failureKind` and `lastError` from the nack and the attempt still counted. It is not claimable until its jittered backoff elapses, so the terminal path below uses a fresh task.

item.name: Enqueue js task (demo) — for the terminal path

request.description: `retryable: false` is terminal — straight to the DLQ regardless of attempts remaining, `failureKind: handler_terminal`. The flag is set by each handler's classifier, the one party that knows its domain's error shapes: for `http`, `429`/`5xx`/resets/timeouts retry and other `4xx` or an SSRF-blocked target do not; for `llm`, rate limits/`5xx`/timeouts retry and auth failures, refusals and bad requests do not; for `js`, script faults (a `SyntaxError`, a throw, a non-serialisable result, the timeout kill) are terminal — the code will not parse differently in 30 seconds — and only transport failures in the script's own I/O (reset, refused, `EAI_AGAIN`) retry. When `kind` is sent it must agree with `retryable` (`handler_terminal`, `timeout`, `unclassified`, `result_too_large`, `no_handler`, `lease_expired` are terminal; `handler_error` and `worker_shutdown` retry), otherwise 422.

exec: pm.test('triage projection omits payload and result', () => {

request.description: `{ tasks, nextCursor }`, newest failures first, keyset-paginated on `(failedAt, id)` so requeueing while paging never skips a row. `limit` 1–100 (default 20); pass `nextCursor` back as `?cursor=` for the next page (`null` on the last). Triage projection only — `id, queue, type, state, attempts, maxAttempts, failureKind, lastError, createdAt, succeededAt, failedAt` — payload and result are deliberately omitted (they carry code, prompts and credentials); drill in with `GET /tasks/:id`. 404 for a queue that does not exist.

No body, no worker header (the UI's per-row action). Replays a dead-lettered task: back to `ready` immediately, attempts and forgiveness reset to 0, failure fields cleared. 204 on success; 404 for an unknown id; 409 `not-in-dlq` if the task exists but is not dead-lettered.

item.name: 5. Idempotent enqueue (dedupe) — queue: demo
item.description: Two enqueues sharing a `dedupeKey` within the queue's dedupe window (10min for `demo`) collapse to one task: a partial unique index on `(queue_name, dedupe_key)`, with the insert resolved by `ON CONFLICT` in the same statement, so concurrent producers cannot both win.

request.description: 201 on the first run within a dedupe window; 200 on a re-run inside the window (the key is still live — the reaper releases it once the window lapses). Either way it captures the surviving id.

exec: pm.test('200 — collapsed onto the existing task', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
pm.test('same id as the first enqueue', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().id).to.eql(pm.collectionVariables.get('dedupeId')));

request.description: Returns the first enqueue's id with 200 — no second task is created. The stored payload is the first one's; a differing payload on the duplicate is ignored, not merged.

item.name: 6. Validation & errors
item.description: The negative cases, one per status code. Errors are RFC 9457 problem+json — `{ type: '/problems/<code>', title, status, detail }`, content-type `application/problem+json` — where `type` disambiguates what the status alone cannot (409 covers both a lost lease and a requeue of a non-DLQ task). The map: malformed JSON → 400 `unparseable`; missing/malformed `X-Worker-Id` on a worker endpoint → 400 `missing-worker-id`; forged Host → 400 `bad-host`; unknown task or queue → 404 `not-found`; lost lease → 409 `lost-lease`; requeue of a non-DLQ task → 409 `not-in-dlq`; body over cap → 413 `payload-too-large`; body parses but fails the schema → 422 `validation`. Internal failures are a static 500 `internal` — no driver message ever reaches the caller.

request.description: The body does not parse at all — 400, as distinct from 422 for a body that parses but fails validation.
`type` must be one of `llm`, `js`, `http`. Nothing is created — the queue is not even created implicitly, because validation runs first.

The payload is validated against its own type's schema at the edge; `js` requires a non-empty `source`. Unknown fields anywhere in the body are rejected too, so a typo fails loudly rather than being silently dropped.

exec: // 300 000 bytes: over the 256 KiB payload cap plus the API's 16 KiB envelope margin.

request.description: The pre-request script inflates `source` to 300 KB. Payloads are capped at 256 KiB (`PAYLOAD_MAX_BYTES`) and refused before parsing; stored results have the same cap on `ack`.
`max` is bounded by the deployment's `CLAIM_MAX_LIMIT` (default 100); a request above it is 422, not clamped. An unbounded batch size is a denial-of-service parameter.

item.name: Claim on an unknown queue → 200, empty

request.description: Unlike `stats` and `dlq`, `claim` does not 404 on an unknown queue: it is the highest-frequency endpoint, an unknown queue is indistinguishable from an empty one to a worker, and the existence check would cost a lookup per poll. An empty claim is 200 with `tasks: []` rather than 204, so clients parse one shape.

A blameless (forgiving) nack is inherently retryable; pairing it with `retryable: false` contradicts itself and is rejected at the edge, before the store is touched. When `kind` is sent it must agree with `retryable` (`handler_terminal`, `timeout`, `unclassified`, `result_too_large`, `no_handler`, `lease_expired` are terminal; `handler_error` and `worker_shutdown` retry), otherwise 422.

`claim` carries `workerId` in the body per the brief and `X-Worker-Id` in the header like every worker endpoint; the two must agree, otherwise a worker could claim under one identity and be unable to ack under the other. Nothing is claimed.
The same rule as `claim`: body `workerId` and header `X-Worker-Id` must agree; `extend` is the other endpoint the brief gives a body `workerId`.

Re-acks the task folder 3 already acked (run folder 3 first). The task exists, so 404 would be false — what is gone is the caller's claim on it. The same 409 answers an ack, nack or extend from a worker whose lease lapsed and was re-claimed, or one echoing a stale `claimId`.

item.name: Requeue a task not in the DLQ → 409

request.description: Same status as a lost lease, different `type` — the task folder 3 acked is `succeeded`, not dead-lettered, so there is nothing to replay.
A well-formed UUID that names no task. An id that is not a UUID at all is 422 instead.
`stats` and `dlq` 404 on a queue that does not exist; only enqueue creates queues implicitly. Queue names must match `[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,128}` (422 otherwise).

The worker endpoints (claim/ack/nack/extend) require `X-Worker-Id` matching `[A-Za-z0-9._-]{1,128}`; this omits it and is rejected before any handler or body parsing runs. Producers, reads and requeue need no header.

A DNS-rebinding control: a page that rebinds its own domain to this API's address is same-origin, so CORS never fires — the Host header is the signal that survives. Anything outside loopback and `ALLOWED_HOSTS` is rejected on every path, static and health included. Postman may flag the overridden Host with a warning — it is still sent.

item.name: 7. Load generator — watch ready climb
item.description: Click Send once: the pre-request script reads `ready` on the unworked `demo` queue, then fires `loadCount` (default 50) enqueues into it. The tasks carry no `dedupeKey` and have distinct sources, so none collapse; nothing consumes `demo`, so `ready` climbs by exactly `loadCount` and holds — the test asserts that exact climb and that every enqueue returned 201. Then open the dashboard at `baseUrl` and watch. Bump `loadCount` to spam harder. (Later manual claims in folders 3–4 pick these up oldest-first, which is fine — every flow captures the id it actually claimed.)

exec: // pm.variables resolves like {{...}} does, so an environment override of baseUrl reaches this script too.
pm.sendRequest({ url: base + '/queues/' + queue + '/stats', method: 'GET' }, (err, res) => {
if (err) { console.log('stats before the load failed: ' + err); return; }
else { console.log('stats before the load returned ' + res.code); return; }
body: { mode: 'raw', raw: JSON.stringify({ type: 'js', payload: { source: 'return ' + i + ';' } }) }
if (++done === count) console.log('enqueued ' + count + ' tasks into ' + queue + ', ' + failures + ' failed — open the UI and watch ready');
console.log('demo ready before: ' + before + ', after: ' + s.ready + ', loadCount: ' + count + ', enqueue failures: ' + failures);
pm.test('stats were read before the load', () => pm.expect(before, 'loadReadyBefore').to.be.a('number').and.not.NaN);
pm.test('ready climbed by exactly loadCount', () => pm.expect(s.ready).to.equal(before + count));

request.description: The pre-request script first records `ready` into `loadReadyBefore` (a 404 — queue not created yet — counts as 0), then enqueues `loadCount` distinct `js` tasks with no `dedupeKey`, so none collapse, counting non-201 responses into `loadFailures`. The sandbox waits for those outstanding `sendRequest` calls before sending this one, so it reads `demo`'s stats after the bulk enqueue. Nothing works `demo`, and `ready` counts delayed and backing-off tasks too, so nothing leaves the count between the two reads: the test asserts `loadFailures` is 0 and `ready` equals `loadReadyBefore + loadCount` exactly. The UI (polling every 2s) shows the same climb.
